records.summaryDescription: This is a colour copy of an illustration Reid did for his 1972 Situationist-inspired publication The Cat Book. This was published pre-Suburban Press and Sex Pistols, but mused on the same themes of upsetting the malaise in the current order. This printing was possibly created to be used in Sex Pistols artwork, but never progressed beyond the copy. Jamie Reid's cut-and-paste aesthetic developed from his interest in radical politics. His artistic style developed while at art college in Croydon, where he was influenced by the ideas of the avant-garde political group, the Situationist International. The political slant to his art was aroused by the May 1968 Paris student riots, which inspired fraternal protests organised by Reid at the Croydon College of Art. These were directed with fellow student Malcolm McLaren, later to become the manager of the Sex Pistols.

galleryLabels.text:
RECORD SLEEVE: NEVER MIND THE BOLLOCKS
HERE'S THE SEX PISTOLS BY THE SEX PISTOLS
Designed by Jamie Reid (British, born 1947)
Issued by Virgin Records Ltd., Great Britain, 1977
Offset lithograph
E/1829-1992

Reid developed his confrontational graphics in the
Suburban Press, a magazine published in Croydon,
1970-75. The DIY ethos of Reid and the archetypal punk
group, The Sex Pistols, energised hundreds of young
designers and musicians disillusioned by the complacency
of the established music and press industries.

records.summaryDescription: This small banner poster was designed by Jamie Reid in order to promote the Sex Pistols' film, and accompanying soundtrack, The Great Rock 'n' Roll Swindle. It uses the symbolic shape and fluorescent colour of the "special offer" flash, often seen in shop windows. This was an element of Reid's earlier anarchic work for the Suburban Press and the Situationist International, and here, subverted commercial and capitalist advertising strategies to promote an album by a group of anarchists. Jamie Reid's cut-and-paste aesthetic, as seen on this poster, developed from his interest in radical politics. His artistic style developed while at art college in Croydon, where he was influenced by the ideas of the avant-garde political group, the Situationist International. The political slant to his art was aroused by the May 1968 Paris student riots, which inspired fraternal protests organised by Reid at the Croydon College of Art. These were directed with fellow student Malcolm McLaren, who would later become the manager of the Sex Pistols.

records.summaryDescription:
This sticker was designed and printed while Jamie Reid was working on the Socialist magazine Suburban Press and distributed to counteract what they saw as propaganda by the government during the miners' strikes and the three day weeks of December 1973 and January 1974. The UK was being told to switch something off and conserve energy, to prove that we didn't need the miners. Reid set out to support the National Union of Mineworkers by promotion of the opposite through guerilla design. 

Jamie Reid's cut-and-paste aesthetic developed from his interest in radical politics. His artistic style developed while at art college in Croydon, where he was influenced by the ideas of the avant-garde political group, the Situationist International. The political slant to his art was aroused by the May 1968 Paris student riots, which inspired fraternal protests organised by Reid at the Croydon College of Art. These were directed with fellow student Malcolm McLaren, who would later become the manager of the Sex Pistols.

records.summaryDescription: Jamie Reid's cut-and-paste aesthetic developed from his interest in radical politics. His artistic style developed while at art college in Croydon, where he was influenced by the ideas of the avant-garde political group, the Situationist International. The political slant to his art was aroused by the May 1968 Paris student riots, which inspired fraternal protests organised by Reid at the Croydon College of Art. These were directed with fellow student Malcolm McLaren (1946-2010), later to become the manager of the Sex Pistols. Reid followed art college by starting his own left-wing small press publisher, Suburban Press, unearthing political intrigue and spreading the ideas of the Situationists through his graphics, employing their ideas of détournement, lettrism and sloganeering. Détournement, a method using well-known media to create a new work with a different message, is central to Reid’s Sex Pistols work, epitomised in his use of images of the Queen defaced with safety pins and swastikas. Lettrism – the incorporation of letters, numerals and non-Western calligraphy into painting to fuse art with poetry, is also abundant, as is his use of sloganeering in repeated statements such as ‘Never Trust a Hippie’, and ‘Anarchy Is The Key’.
